title: Blueprints
subtitle: A House Made of Ideas
summary: Bea's mother was an architect who died when Bea was five. In the attic of their Chicago apartment, Bea finds her mother's old sketchbook — full of drawings of an impossible house. She decides to build it, room by room, in miniature. Each drawing has a note in the margin. Each note tells her something about the person she barely remembers.

paragraphs: The apartment where Bea lived with her father was on the top floor of an old brick building in Chicago, and above their apartment was an attic that no one ever went into. It had a low sloped ceiling and a single round window at the far end that looked out at the roofs of the neighborhood. Her father kept old tax papers and Christmas boxes up there, and he had told Bea once that she was not to go in alone, because he had never checked the floorboards.

But it was the second week of summer, and Bea was eleven, and her father was at work at the university, and she had been reading a book about an English girl who found a magic garden in the ruins of a manor house. When she closed the book, she thought about the attic. She thought about it for a long time. And then she got the small step-stool from the kitchen and she carried it into the hallway, and she pulled the string, and the folding ladder came down.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: close view of a cardboard box on a wooden attic floor, its flaps open, revealing a large leather-bound sketchbook resting on top of folded architectural blueprints. Warm amber overhead light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette. No people visible.
paragraphs: The attic smelled like paper and cedar and a little bit of dust. There were more boxes than Bea had expected. Most were labeled in her father's small square handwriting — TAXES 2018, CHRISTMAS LIGHTS, TOBY (which was the name of a cat they had once had). But behind those, against the far wall under the round window, there was a box that had no label at all. The cardboard was old and soft. The flaps were tucked closed rather than taped.

Bea opened the box. Inside were folded blueprints — big architect's papers, the kind that unfold into sheets almost as wide as she was tall. And on top of the blueprints, in a leather cover that had gone the color of old honey, was a sketchbook. The initials on the cover were R. L. M. Rachel Louisa Marchetti. Her mother's.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: an open architect's sketchbook lying flat, its left page showing a detailed line drawing of an impossible tall house with three stacked floors that appear to twist slightly, spiral stairs on the outside, small circular windows. Right page shows handwritten notes and small arrows pointing at parts of the drawing. Girl's hand visible at the edge of the page. Warm ink drawing style within a warm ink illustration frame. Heavy outlines, cream paper.
paragraphs: Bea sat down on the attic floor with the sketchbook in her lap. She opened it very carefully. She had been told about her mother her whole life — that she had been an architect, that she had loved windows more than walls, that she had died when Bea was five, in a small car accident on the highway coming back from a work trip. Bea had two memories of her mother, or maybe just one and a half. One was the smell of her hair, which was like green tea. The other was a laugh, low and small, that she was not sure she was remembering correctly.

The first page of the sketchbook was a drawing of a house. But it was not a house that could exist. It had three floors, and each floor was slightly rotated from the one below, so the whole building seemed to twist as it went up. There were spiral stairs on the outside, wrapping around. There was a garden on the roof with tiny drawn trees. There was a curved wall on the second floor that had no straight edges at all. And in the margin, in her mother's handwriting — Bea recognized it from the recipe cards her father still kept in the kitchen — there was a note that said: A house should follow the sun. It should not sit still and wait for the sun to come to it.

Bea turned the page. There was another drawing. A room where the walls were bookshelves that went all the way up to the ceiling, and the ceiling was glass, and above the glass ceiling was a small pond, so that anyone lying on the floor of the library and looking up would see the shadows of fish moving across the books. In the margin: For a person who needs to read but does not want to be alone.

She turned another page. A kitchen, but the kitchen table was mounted on a hinge and could be folded up flat against the wall when it was not being used. In the margin: Small rooms should be honest about being small. Give the floor back when you can.

There were forty-two pages. Bea did not read them all. She read enough to understand that the whole book was one house — one impossible house, room by room. And her mother had been designing it, page by page, over many years. The last drawing was dated the month before she died.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: a Chicago apartment kitchen at evening, warm amber lamp light, a man in his early forties (Bea's father) sitting at a small table, holding the leather-bound sketchbook open, looking down at it with a soft still expression. Girl (Bea, 11, short dark hair, cream sweater) standing beside him, watching him. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: When her father got home that evening, Bea had made the kitchen table look normal again and had put the sketchbook in the middle of it, where he could not miss it. He came in, put down his bag, saw the book, and stopped. He did not ask where she had found it. He picked it up and opened it and looked at the first drawing for a long time.

"I didn't know she was still working on it," he said finally. "She never showed me the whole thing. She said it wasn't finished." He looked up at Bea. "Do you want to keep it in your room?" Bea nodded. She was afraid that if she spoke, he would change his mind.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: a child's desk in a bedroom, cluttered with model-building supplies — sheets of foam board in cream and white, small tubes of glue, tiny popsicle sticks, cardboard, a metal ruler, colored pencils, scissors, tweezers. A single lamp lit above the desk. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette. No people visible.
paragraphs: It took her two weeks to get the materials. She used her allowance and the money she had saved from her birthday. She bought foam board at the art store on Belmont, and a metal ruler, and thin balsa wood that was easier to cut than she had expected. She bought good glue and small tweezers and a package of tiny plastic figures the size of her fingernail, meant for architects who wanted to show a person in their models for scale.

She cleared her desk and taped a large piece of paper to it. She had decided she would build the whole house at one-fiftieth scale, which meant a real room ten feet wide would be about two and a half inches in her model. She wrote that at the top of the paper. She wrote her mother's name too, small, in the corner. And then she opened the sketchbook to the first page, and she began.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: close view of a small foam-board model of a curved-wall room being assembled on a wooden desk, glue drying at seams, a bit of pencil-drawn detail on one wall, tiny scale figures of two people placed inside for size. Girl's hand at the edge holding tweezers. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: The first room she built was the curved-wall room from page two. It was harder than she had expected. Foam board did not like to curve. She had to score it, again and again, with the back of her knife, until it would bend without cracking. She got it wrong the first time and threw the whole thing away. She got it wrong the second time and cried a little in the bathroom so her father would not see. On the third try, it curved.

When it was standing on her desk, small and honest and slightly wobbly, she went back to the sketchbook. The note in the margin said: A curved wall makes people slow down. They cannot walk straight across it. This is good in a kitchen. It is bad in a hallway. Bea thought about that. She thought her mother must have watched people walking through rooms and noticed things. She wondered if that was the sort of thing you were born knowing, or if you learned it.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: a child's bedroom viewed from the doorway, one wall completely lined with a growing collection of small foam-board and balsa-wood model rooms — a spiral staircase, a rooftop garden with tiny paper trees, a library with glass ceiling, a folding kitchen. Each one small enough to hold in two hands. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette. No people visible.
paragraphs: She worked on it every day for the rest of June and most of July. Her father asked her, more than once, if she wanted help. She always said no. She was not sure why. It felt like the sort of thing she needed to do alone. Or maybe not quite alone — she was doing it with the sketchbook, and the sketchbook felt, sometimes, like a very quiet person sitting next to her.

The rooms began to line up on the shelf above her desk. The spiral staircase, made from thin balsa strips glued to a paper tube. The library with the glass ceiling, which she made from a piece of clear plastic she cut from a strawberry container. The kitchen with the folding table, whose hinge she made from a bent paperclip. The rooftop garden with tiny paper trees, each one no bigger than a grain of rice. Every time she finished one, she read the note in the margin, and she wrote the note on a small card, and she taped the card to the room.

She began to know things about her mother that she had not known before. Her mother thought children should have their own doors. Every room she designed for a child had a small second door, low to the floor. "So they can leave when they need to," she had written. "And so they can come back in without asking."
Her mother hated corridors. "A corridor is space that has been wasted," one note said. "If you must have one, make it a room. Put a window in it. Put a chair in it. Give it a reason to exist."

Her mother liked ceilings that were low in some places and high in others. She thought this was truer to how people actually wanted to feel. "You are cozy where the ceiling is low," she wrote. "You breathe where it is high."
Bea began to think that if she had known her mother longer, they might have agreed on a lot of things.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: a small model of a corner room being placed on a shelf next to other completed model rooms. This one has a small round window and a low doorway. Girl's hands (Bea, 11) carefully placing it. Warm amber light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: By the last week of July, she had built twenty-nine of the forty-two rooms. She had one to go before the very last one, and she had been saving it because she was a little afraid of it. It was the room on the second-to-last page, and it did not have any furniture drawn in. It was very small, and shaped like a corner, and it had a round window and a low door. In the margin, her mother had written just three words: For a small one.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: close view of the last page of an old leather sketchbook lying open on a wooden desk. The drawing shows a small square room with all four walls solid — but each wall is drawn with a thick outline of a window shape inside it. Handwritten notes in the margin. Girl's hand at the edge. Warm amber lamp light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: The last page of the sketchbook was a room she could not figure out how to build. The drawing showed a small square room, and each of the four walls had, drawn inside it, the thick outline of a window. But the windows were not open — they were part of the walls. They were the same material as the walls. Bea did not understand what she was supposed to make.

The note in the margin said this: A room where the walls become windows at night. Not for looking out. For looking through — at everything at once. This is a room for someone who is going to grow up in the middle of everything, and who will need, sometimes, to see all of it. This is a room for our second child. When she comes. If she comes. — R.

Bea sat at her desk for a long time. She read the note four times. Then five. She was the second child. She had a brother named Nico who was in college now, seven years older than her. Her mother had drawn this room, and written this note, before Bea was born. It was Bea's room. It had always been Bea's room, waiting on the last page of the book for her to find it.

She did not build the room that night. She closed the sketchbook and got into bed and lay on her back and looked at the ceiling of her actual bedroom, which was plain white plaster with a small crack near the light fixture. She tried to think about what walls that became windows at night might mean. She tried to think about it the way her mother would have. She could not.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: a father (early 40s) and daughter (Bea, 11) sitting side by side at her desk, both looking at the open sketchbook. The father is holding a pencil and pointing at something on the page. Warm evening lamp light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: In the morning she showed the page to her father. She had not shown him anything else she had built. All the model rooms were still on her shelf and she had let him see them but not asked him about them. But this drawing she brought to him at the breakfast table, and she put it in front of his cereal bowl, and she said, "I don't know how to build this one."

Her father looked at it for a long time. He read the margin note. He put down his spoon. "Oh, Bea," he said, very quietly. And then, after another long moment, he said, "I think I know what she meant. Get your pencils."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: father and daughter sitting on the bedroom floor together, working on a small model room. Around them: bits of clear plastic, thin dark paper, glue, a pencil. The model in front of them is a small square room with plain-looking walls. Warm afternoon light through a real window in the background. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: They sat on her bedroom floor and they built it together. It took them all afternoon. Her father cut four square walls out of foam board. Then, on the inside of each wall, he showed her how to glue a thin sheet of dark paper. And then he took a needle and, very carefully, he pricked hundreds of tiny holes through the paper, in the shapes of leaves, and trees, and city streets, and a river, and a cloud, and a bird. "When the room is dark," he said, "and there is a candle in the middle, the light will come through the holes. And the walls will look like windows."

"How did you know?" Bea asked. Her father did not answer right away. He kept pricking holes. He was doing the shape of a boat now, small and careful, in the middle of one wall. "She told me once," he said. "When she was pregnant with you. She said she was going to design a room for you where you could see everything without leaving. She said she wanted you to know that being inside and being outside were not opposites." He looked up. "I forgot until you showed me the drawing. I'm sorry I forgot."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: a small square model room sitting on a dark table in a dimly lit bedroom. Inside the model, a single tiny candle burns. Its light shines through hundreds of small pinpricks in the walls, projecting patterns of leaves, birds, and small stars onto the surrounding table and the child's face leaning close to look. Girl's face (Bea, 11) partly lit from the model. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, warm cream and gold palette with cool dark surroundings.
paragraphs: They finished at dusk. Her father put a small birthday-cake candle in the middle of the tiny room and lit it, and Bea turned off her bedroom light. And the walls of the little room lit up. Tiny pinprick birds flew across her ceiling. Tiny pinprick trees swayed on her wall. A tiny river ran along the floor. She could see, from inside her one small square, all of it at once — a whole world made only of light and shadow.

"It works," said her father. His voice sounded strange. Bea did not turn to look at him. She thought he might be crying, and she did not want to embarrass him. She sat on the floor of her real room and looked at the small room she had built with her mother's drawings and her father's hands, and she watched the tiny lights move on her walls, and she thought about all the years her mother had spent designing a place that Bea would grow up in. Not the room itself. The idea of the room. The idea that she would need it.

She thought about that for a long time. Then she blew out the candle. She kept the little room on her desk, and she never took it down, not even when she got older and moved into another apartment and then another one after that. It went with her. In the years to come, when she needed to remember that being inside and being outside were not opposites, she would put a candle in it, and she would sit with her back against the wall, and she would watch her mother's world go by.
